```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(exactcond)
```

## The idea

A nuisance parameter is removed by conditioning on a statistic that is sufficient for it. What
remains carries no nuisance, so a reference distribution drawn from it is exact at every sample
size: no asymptotic approximation and no bootstrap. The package supplies two such conditionings,
each sampled by a pure-C back-end in which every replicate draws from its own random stream, so a
result does not depend on the number of threads.

## Two-way tables with both margins fixed

In an $r \times c$ table the row and column totals are sufficient for the marginal parameters.
Given both, the table follows the Fisher-Yates (multivariate hypergeometric) law, which is sampled
exactly by permuting the column labels of the individual observations.

For nominal rows against an ordinal column, the default statistic is the dispersion of the row
mean scores. Its components are the group contrasts themselves, so a significant result points
directly at the rows that differ.

```{r}
tab <- matrix(c(3, 228, 72,
                10, 548, 67,
                7, 276, 131), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE)
ec_rc_test(tab, v = c(-1, 0, 1), B = 5000, seed = 1)
```

When both classifications are ordered, `stat = "linlin"` gives Goodman's (1979)
linear-by-linear association, and `"pearson"` and `"lr"` give the familiar unordered statistics
referred to the exact conditional law rather than to the chi-square.

```{r}
ec_rc_test(tab, stat = "linlin", B = 5000, seed = 1)$p.value
```

The reference distribution itself is available for any margins.

```{r}
null <- ec_rc_null(rows = c(30, 40), cols = c(35, 35), stat = "pearson", B = 2000, seed = 2)
quantile(null, c(0.5, 0.95))
```

`ec_pvalue()` turns an observed value and a sample from the null into a p-value, a mid-p value and
a Monte Carlo interval for the p-value.

```{r}
str(ec_pvalue(quantile(null, 0.95), null))
```

## Do two tables share an association?

`ec_rc_two()` conditions further on the total score, which cancels a common association
parameter. The result is a test, free of any nuisance parameter, of whether two tables share it.
The conditional law is sampled by a Markov chain (hence `burn` and `thin`); the function reports
the conditional mid-p value and the size attainable at `alpha`, since the law is discrete.

```{r}
a <- matrix(c(20, 8, 3, 9, 22, 7, 4, 8, 19), 3, byrow = TRUE)
b <- matrix(c(18, 9, 4, 8, 20, 8, 5, 9, 18), 3, byrow = TRUE)
r2 <- ec_rc_two(a, b, B = 2000, seed = 3)
c(midp = r2$midp, size = r2$size)
```

## Linear models after the structure was chosen by fit

In a linear model under a null in which the tested structure is absent, any statistic that is
invariant to the coefficients and to the error scale depends on the data only through the residual
direction, and that direction is uniform on the unit sphere of the residual space. So the
reference stays exact when the statistic is the maximum over several candidate structures, for
instance several spatial weight matrices, one of which was chosen because it fitted best.

`ec_sphere_maxquad()` samples the maximum over candidate matrices of the normalised quadratic form
in the residual direction.

```{r}
n <- 12
X <- cbind(1, seq_len(n))
M <- diag(n) - X %*% solve(crossprod(X), t(X))
A <- diag(n)[, c(n, seq_len(n - 1))]
A <- (A + t(A)) / 2
quantile(ec_sphere_maxquad(M, A, B = 2000, seed = 4), 0.95)
```

## Permutation tests for batteries and networks

Two permutation tests use the same back-end. They refer a statistic to the law obtained by
permuting group labels, across individuals or across clusters (exchangeability blocks in the sense
of Winkler et al., 2014).

`ec_multi_test()` tests a battery of categorical items across groups with one p-value: the sum or
the maximum over items of a per-item statistic, in the spirit of Pesarin and Salmaso's (2010)
nonparametric combination. Per-item p-values come from the same permutations, so they can be used
for a closed follow-up.

```{r}
set.seed(2)
g <- rep(c("a", "b", "c"), c(60, 80, 60))
x <- cbind(rbinom(200, 1, 0.9), rbinom(200, 1, 0.95),
           rbinom(200, 1, ifelse(g == "c", 0.7, 0.9)))   # only item 3 differs
r <- ec_multi_test(x, g, B = 2000, seed = 1)
r
r$items
```

`ec_diffnet_test()` compares correlation networks across groups without a Gaussian assumption. The
edge statistic is the heterogeneity of the Fisher-transformed correlations. The network statistic
is their sum or maximum over edges, as in the Network Comparison Test of van Borkulo et al. (2023).
With `rank = TRUE` the procedure is distribution-free.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
n <- 120; p <- 5
g <- rep(c("a", "b"), each = n / 2)
z <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), n)
z[g == "b", 2] <- 0.8 * z[g == "b", 1] + 0.6 * z[g == "b", 2]
ec_diffnet_test(z, g, B = 999, seed = 1)
```

## References

Goodman, L. A. (1979). Simple models for the analysis of association in cross-classifications
having ordered categories. *Journal of the American Statistical Association*, 74, 537-552.
doi:10.1080/01621459.1979.10481650

Pesarin, F. and Salmaso, L. (2010). *Permutation Tests for Complex Data*. Wiley.
doi:10.1002/9780470689516

van Borkulo, C. D., van Bork, R., Boschloo, L., Kossakowski, J. J., Tio, P., Schoevers, R. A.,
Borsboom, D. and Waldorp, L. J. (2023). Comparing network structures on three aspects: a
permutation test. *Psychological Methods*, 28, 1273-1285. doi:10.1037/met0000476

Winkler, A. M., Ridgway, G. R., Webster, M. A., Smith, S. M. and Nichols, T. E. (2014).
Permutation inference for the general linear model. *NeuroImage*, 92, 381-397.
doi:10.1016/j.neuroimage.2014.01.060
